      RESEARCH
      Learning physical systems for control and optimization.
      My research asks which physical variables a learned model must represent, how those states evolve under external forcing and incomplete observation, and which approximation errors change the resulting schedule, control action, or design. I study this question through probabilistic prediction, neural operators, closed-loop analysis, and constrained optimization.
    
    
      
        Decision-focused forecasting under uncertainty
        Probabilistic forecasts are trained and evaluated through the schedules, costs, and constraints they induce. Work on water-demand timing and uncertain pressure regression further identifies when prediction errors occur and which unobserved effects they represent.
      
      
        Neural operators for distributed dynamics
        I study maps from initial conditions, geometry, boundary conditions, and forcing fields to spatiotemporal solutions. Field error, rollout error, and sensitivity error measure how accurately the learned operator represents the dynamics used in control and optimization.
      
      
        Learning-based control
        I examine how approximation error accumulates over a control horizon and changes the selected action, closed-loop cost, and constraint violation. These quantities provide control-specific criteria for training and evaluating learned physical dynamics.
      
      
        Constrained optimization of physical systems
        I study differentiable solution operators inside constrained design and operating problems, including experiment selection, process control, and materials design. Gradient accuracy and feasibility determine whether the learned model preserves the optimized decision.

title: Temporal response and uncertain pressure states
text: Urban water systems are observed through demand and pressure time series. Average prediction error does not reveal whether a model responds late to a changing demand trajectory or misses pressure variation associated with an unobserved disturbance. The two studies below isolate these sources of error.

title: Temporal response and uncertain pressure states
text:
Demand dynamics near turning points
Daily urban water demand is nonlinear and nonstationary. The knowledge-based bi-correction model focuses on forecast lag near turning points, where the predicted response follows a change in demand too late. Lag-penalty attention extracts sequence and feature information associated with timely demand changes. A stacked LSTM produces the primary forecast, after which a masked weighted Markov chain corrects selected residuals using posterior error information.

title: Temporal response and uncertain pressure states
text:
Evaluation of response timing
The study introduces mean prediction trend effectiveness to test whether the predicted trend improves on a naive forecast. Reporting this quantity with absolute-error metrics distinguishes delayed response near a turning point from numerical error in demand magnitude.

title: Temporal response and uncertain pressure states
text:
Pressure response under unobserved disturbances
CritiCoder models macroscopic pressure when measured variables do not explain every disturbance in a water distribution system. The Coder approximates the pressure response associated with observed variables. By changing the loss, the Critic represents the remaining variation as a distribution of uncertain disturbances associated with unobserved variables.

title: Temporal response and uncertain pressure states
text:
Evaluation of disturbance sensitivity
The node-level comparison tests pressure monitors with different disturbance strengths. At nodes more strongly affected by unobserved disturbances, CritiCoder shows a smaller decline in predictive performance than the tested regression baselines.

title: Temporal response and uncertain pressure states
section: Relation to Physical AI for Science
text:
Relation to Physical AI for Science
The studies resolve two properties of the state information supplied to later scheduling or control. KbBcM tests whether a sequence model follows the direction of demand change at the correct time. CritiCoder tests how pressure prediction behaves when measured inputs leave part of the variation unresolved. Together, they represent response timing and residual state uncertainty at the level of the urban water system.

title: Research
text:
My research in Physical AI for Science examines how learned models represent state evolution under physical constraints and incomplete information. The state may be a temporal quantity such as demand or pressure, or a distributed field defined by initial conditions, geometry, boundary conditions, and external forcing. I evaluate a learned representation through the operating schedule, control action, or physical design computed from it.
The same research question appears in four settings. Decision-focused forecasting links temporal uncertainty to operating cost. Neural operators approximate maps from physical conditions to spatiotemporal state fields. Learning-based control measures how rollout error changes closed-loop behavior. Constrained optimization tests whether the learned solution map supplies accurate sensitivities and feasible designs. Each direction traces the same relation among physical dynamics, learned representation, and downstream decision.

title: Research
text:
Decision-focused forecasting under uncertainty
Forecast errors matter differently when predictions determine an operating schedule. In coupled water–energy systems, Stochastic Predict-Then-Optimize trains probabilistic electricity-cost forecasts through the stochastic water-supply schedules they induce. A differentiable upper bound on optimality gap passes changes in scheduling cost back to the predictor.
Work on lag-free demand forecasting and uncertain pressure regression examines two additional sources of prediction error. Lag-penalty attention targets delayed reactions near demand turning points, while uncertain regression separates modeled responses to observed inputs from residual pressure variation associated with unobserved disturbances. Their metrics distinguish response timing and disturbance sensitivity from average numerical error.

title: Research
text:
Neural operators for distributed dynamics
Many control and design problems depend on physical fields that evolve across space and time. I study neural operators that map initial conditions, geometry, boundary conditions, and forcing fields to spatiotemporal solution fields. Their evaluation includes field error, rollout error, and the sensitivities used by control and optimization.

title: Research
text:
Learning-based control
A learned solution operator can supply state rollouts without solving the governing equations from scratch at every control step. I study how approximation error accumulates over a control horizon and changes the selected action, closed-loop cost, and constraint violation. These quantities provide control-specific criteria for training and evaluating learned physical dynamics.

title: Research
text:
Constrained optimization and materials processes
Constrained optimization depends on accurate state trajectories, local sensitivities, and feasible decisions. I study differentiable solution operators inside design and operating problems, with attention to whether surrogate gradients preserve the selected decision. Objective value, feasibility, and decision sensitivity provide the main evaluation quantities.
Materials processes provide a field-evolving setting for this work. Learned solution maps can support experiment selection, process control, and constrained design when the physical state evolves across space and time.

title: Research
text:
Related collaborative work
Collaborative work on generated actions examines how learned trajectories satisfy geometric and decision constraints. DRIFT stores local LiDAR geometry as graph memory during recurrent diffusion and evaluates the generated motion through endpoint error, clearance, smoothness, and runtime.

title: Coupled water-energy operation under forecast uncertainty
text:
Urban water supply coordinates treatment, transport, and distribution over an operating horizon. Each stage consumes electricity, so the schedule determines when the system serves demand and purchases energy. Because electricity prices are uncertain, a forecast error can alter both operating cost and the selected schedule.
The study represents the full water-supply process as a stochastic scheduling problem. Within this formulation, a probabilistic electricity-cost forecast supplies the uncertain cost parameters, while the scheduling model retains the operating variables and constraints. Optimizing the schedule returns a decision loss to the predictor. Training focuses on errors that change when the system operates, rather than treating every price error as equally consequential.

title: Coupled water-energy operation under forecast uncertainty
text:
Learning through the induced schedule
Stochastic Predict-Then-Optimize trains the forecast distribution through the optimality gap of the induced schedule. Its training signal depends on how an error changes the selected operating periods and their cost. This decision loss ties the predictor to the temporal coupling between water operation and grid conditions.

title: Coupled water-energy operation under forecast uncertainty
text:
Differentiable optimality gap
Direct differentiation through stochastic scheduling is difficult. SPTO+ derives a differentiable convex upper bound on the optimality gap from Lagrangian duality. The bound supplies a surrogate gradient while the scheduling problem remains the source of the learning signal.

title: Coupled water-energy operation under forecast uncertainty
text:
System-level evaluation
Experiments on real-world water-supply systems compare pointwise forecast error, operating cost, and decision regret with tested two-stage forecasting and optimization baselines. SPTO reports lower operating cost and regret in these experiments.

title: Coupled water-energy operation under forecast uncertainty
section: Relation to Physical AI for Science
text:
Relation to Physical AI for Science
In the coupled system, the learned distribution parameterizes the uncertain energy cost acting on a temporally coordinated water process. A constrained optimizer converts those parameters into a feasible operating schedule. Decision regret then measures the consequence of forecast error at the system level.

title: Research projects
text:
My research examines how a learned model should represent the state and evolution of a physical system when its output is used in control or optimization. The starting point is the physical quantity to be predicted or reconstructed, together with the inputs, geometry, constraints, and unresolved disturbances that shape its evolution. I then ask which approximation errors alter the resulting schedule, feedback action, trajectory, or design.
Across these projects, the physical system defines admissible states and decisions. Learning estimates a quantity that is uncertain or costly to obtain, and control or optimization converts that estimate into an action. Evaluation includes the error that matters at the decision level, such as optimality gap, operating cost, constraint violation, or trajectory geometry.

title: Research projects
section: Neural operators for distributed physical dynamics
text:
Neural operators for distributed physical dynamics
My current work studies neural operators that map initial conditions, geometry, boundary conditions, and external forcing to spatiotemporal state fields. This formulation treats the target as a solution map rather than a single operating point. I evaluate field reconstruction, rollout accuracy, and local sensitivities because each quantity affects a downstream control or constrained optimization problem.
Materials processes provide a field-evolving scientific setting for this work. Their states change across space and time, while process inputs determine the trajectory and the resulting operating or design decision. The scientific question is whether a learned operator preserves the field evolution and response derivatives required to select that decision.

title: Research projects
section: Feedback laws for constrained nonlinear dynamics
text:
Feedback laws for constrained nonlinear dynamics


 


Two last-author studies examine learned feedback laws for nonlinear dynamics. For discrete-time constrained systems, nonlinear model predictive control supplies initial weights for a controller network, while a control barrier function and a nonquadratic loss impose state and input constraints during learning. Related adaptive optimal-control work uses eligibility traces at several time scales so that the critic receives temporal credit over different horizons.
Constrained controller · Multiple time-scale eligibility traces

title: Research projects
section: Multi-step energy dynamics in industrial rolling
text:
Multi-step energy dynamics in industrial rolling





Hot-strip roughing unfolds through an ordered sequence of rolling passes in which prediction error can accumulate. A DCLS-Net study models the energy consumption of each pass, while series concatenation propagates information through the rolling order to reduce accumulated multi-step error. The process trajectory, rather than an isolated sample, is the relevant prediction object.

title: Research projects
text:
Geometry-conditioned motion in physical environments





DRIFT stores local LiDAR geometry as graph memory and retrieves waypoint-specific context during recurrent diffusion. Endpoint error, clearance, smoothness, and runtime test how the generated trajectory relates to target intent and local spatial structure. This collaborative project asks how an action generator should retain the geometry that constrains motion, a related question in Physical AI.
